title: Mayi medhām: understanding, offspring and splendour
theme: A threefold prayer that Agni, Indra and Sūrya place in the speaker understanding and offspring, with radiance, strength and brilliance.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «वेदशास्त्रादिग्रन्थग्रहणधारणपटुत्वं» — skill in grasping and retaining the Vedas and śāstras
The anonymous commentator: «प्रजामच्छिन्नसंततिं» — an unbroken line of descendants
The anonymous commentator: «तेजो ब्रह्मवर्चसम्» — the lustre of sacred learning
The anonymous commentator: «इन्द्रियं धातुक्षयादिराहित्येन वीर्यपुष्टिम्» — vigour, free of the wasting of the body
The anonymous commentator: a brilliance of face that unsettles an enemy at a glance

sandhi.type: i before a dissimilar vowel; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: mayi + agniḥ → mayy agniḥ (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)); agniḥ + tejaḥ → agnis tejaḥ (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)).

sandhi.type: i + i; aḥ before a vowel
sandhi.rule: mayi + indraḥ → mayīndraḥ (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)); indraḥ + indriyam → indra indriyam (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
-aḥ becomes -o before bh and before d (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)); the recitation writes the r of sūrya as the Vedic ऱ.

morphology.note: The base writes the r with the Vedic sign ऱ (sūrya); the two other witnesses write र, which the collation lists as spelling only.

translation.literal: In me understanding, in me offspring, in me may Agni place radiance; in me understanding, in me offspring, in me may Indra place strength; in me understanding, in me offspring, in me may Sūrya place brilliance.
translation.readable: May Agni place in me understanding, descendants and the lustre of learning; may Indra place in me understanding, descendants and strength; may the Sun place in me understanding, descendants and brilliance.

anvaya: अग्निः मयि मेधाम् मयि प्रजाम् मयि तेजः दधातु । इन्द्रः मयि मेधाम् मयि प्रजाम् मयि इन्द्रियम् दधातु । सूऱ्यः मयि मेधाम् मयि प्रजाम् मयि भ्राजः दधातु ।
syntax: Three parallel sentences, each with the locative mayi repeated three times, two shared objects (medhām, prajām), a subject (Agni, Indra, Sūrya), a third object proper to that god, and the imperative dadhātu.

ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator: the repetition of mayi and the rest shows the speaker’s earnestness («आदराभिद्योतिका मयिपदाद्यावृत्तिः»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose formula (yajus) in three parallel clauses.

beginner: This short prayer has three parts that repeat a pattern. Each asks a god to place three things in the speaker: understanding, descendants, and a gift proper to that god. From Agni, the fire, it asks the radiance of a learned person; from Indra, king of the gods, strength and vigour; from the Sun, a brilliance that others notice. The words ‘in me’ come again and again. The old commentator says the repetition shows how earnestly the speaker asks. It closes the group of prayers for medhā that began two sections earlier.
analogy: Like asking three different mentors for the same two things, and one more that each is best at giving.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Agni, Indra and Sūrya each to place in the speaker understanding and offspring, and, respectively, radiance, strength and brilliance.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: again, for the sake of medhā and the rest, Agni, Indra and Sūrya are entreated («पुनरपि मेधादिसिद्धयेऽग्नीन्द्रसूर्यान्प्रार्थयते»); medhā is skill in grasping and retaining the Vedas and śāstras, prajā an unbroken line of descendants, tejas the lustre of sacred learning; the rest needs no explanation («निगदव्याख्यातमन्यत्»).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this formula, which may not be in their recensions; Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The prayer names exactly what it asks for, three times over. Saying clearly what one hopes for, and from whom, can itself clarify the hope. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you could ask for three things for the people who come after you, what would they be?
reflect.deeper: Why might understanding and descendants be asked for together, again and again?
reflect.practice: Write down the one quality you most hope to pass on, and one thing you can do this week to pass it on.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it.
